Fagnano

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: A triangle can hold another triangle with one corner on each side; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the six dots to change the two triangles. Tick the boxes for names or altitude lines, or press the button to put the three side dots at the feet of the altitudes.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step). The first three dots set the outer triangle; the others stay on its sides.

Look for the math

In 1775 Fagnano asked for the triangle of smallest perimeter that fits inside a given acute triangle. The surprising answer is that the three corners must be the feet of the altitudes. The applet draws the same rolling picture that Schwarz used to prove it. Its page now shows a Wolfram Demonstration instead of the Java applet (the original applet tag is commented out in the page source); the geometry here follows the archived applet and the written proof on that page.

The answer is the altitude feet

Let P lie on BC, Q on CA and R on AB. The orthic triangle joins the three altitude feet. The page claims it is the unique smallest-perimeter inscribed triangle of an acute triangle. The logic test confirms this on 250 acute triangles by searching along BC, and on 12 more by a full grid search over all three side positions: no sampled triangle beats the orthic one. Press the button to see the red path become a single straight line.

Schwarz rolls the triangle five times

Reflect the triangle in CA, then in the new BC, then AB, CA, BC again. The six copies form a chain, and the page says the final AB is parallel to the first with the same direction. The three sides of PQR reappear as the six red pieces. When PQR is orthic, the pieces join into one straight segment of length 2 × perimeter(orthic); every other choice gives a longer bent path. The test checked this on 600 acute triangles: the parallel claim and the doubled length held every time. One small port quirk: the Java code uses a shortcut when a mirror side is within one board unit of vertical, which can shift the drawing a little; the page's claim is about true reflections, and the test checks both the true chain and the applet's shorthand.

Fejér's two reflections

Reflect P in CA and in AB, giving P' and P''. For a fixed P, the shortest route P'Q + QR + RP'' is the straight line P'P'', so Q and R must obey the mirror rule. The page notes that angle P'AP'' = 2A wherever P sits and that AP' = AP, so P'P'' = 2 AP sin(A). That is shortest when AP is an altitude, which makes BQ perpendicular to CA and CR perpendicular to AB. All three identities were checked on 600 configurations and held to within a billionth of a board unit.

Other triangles, other pages

The page adds that for right or obtuse triangles no proper inscribed triangle reaches the minimum: perimeters can get arbitrarily close to twice the shortest altitude. A search of 24 such triangles agreed, with the closest approaches all collapsed onto a vertex. This is the original Fagnano problem page: Fagnano III (Samelson's solution) and Fagnano IV (Izvolsky's circumcenter and area bound 2 Area / R) are different proofs on their own pages, not what this applet draws. The Java let a dragged side dot wander off its side; this illustration keeps it on the side, since only inscribed triangles are relevant to the claim.

Try this: make a tall, thin triangle, note the red path length, then press the button and watch the six pieces snap into a single line.
